newsitem.title: CHILE: U.S. dumping rules may contravene WTO --Chile.
newsitem.headline: U.S. dumping rules may contravene WTO --Chile.

text.p: Chile may ask the World Trade Organization to study U.S. anti-dumping rules after claims by U.S. salmon raisers that Chilean producers are dumping fish in the American market, said Foreign Minister Jose Miguel Insulza.

"We are under the impression that the North American anti-dumping mechanisms are contrary to WTO (rules) and we want to explore the possibility of consultation with the United States to this organization," said Insulza by telephone from Singapore where he is on an official visit.
Insulza said Chile's ambassador in Washington, John Biehl, has already contacted the Commerce Department to put the Chilean government's case in the dispute.

Economy Minister Alvaro Garcia was due to travel to Washington next week to hold talks with Commerce Secretary William Daley over the spat, Chile's most serious trade dispute in recent years with the United States.

U.S. salmon raisers have accused Chilean producers of dumping and of receiving illegal subsidies from the government. To prove dumping charges, the accuser must generally show the producer is selling below cost, or below the cost at which it sells its product in its home market.
The American companies were due to present their allegations to the Commerce Department and the International Trade Organization in mid-July.
Insulza stressed that the salmon dispute was not caused by the U.S. government but was the result of protectionism from American salmon companies.
"I believe that the government of the United States has the best intention of developing satisfactorily its trade relationship with Chile," said Insulza.
"The problem is the presentation made by North American salmon companies."

In the past 15 years, Chile has become a major producer of farmed salmon. Output has gone from virtually zero in the late 1970s to about 100,000 tonnes in 1995, making it the world's second largest producer of farmed salmon after Norway.
U.S. consumers account for 30 percent of Chile's total salmon exports, with shipments to the American market worth around $180 million.
In a separate case, Chilean officials have alleged that a recent federal court ruling forbidding the U.S. government from issuing new import permits for logs and wood from Chile broke WTO rules.

"The federal judge's order and the interpretation by the Agriculture Department violate international accords signed by the United States, in particular the WTO's agreement on sanitary measures," said Agriculture Minister Carlos Mladinic.
Mladinic said the ruling could hit exports worth around $100 million in the next few years.
